title: POC Weekly - Latency Tuning - LakeshoreBank
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest latency benchmarks (TTFT, streaming), discuss kernel choices and sequence length tradeoffs, agree next steps for a 1k-query benchmark and canary deployment. Agreed to enable streaming, test kernel variant B, and reduce max seqlen for critical path. Jordan to share updated bench spreadsheet and pricing notes.
meeting_header:
Date: 2027-10-19
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Leah (Redwood CSM), Maya (Lakeshore Eng Mgr), Carlos (Product), Priya (SRE)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this tight - 45 minutes. Quick realign: goal is to go over last week's latency runs and decide next tuning steps.
[00:22] Maya (Lakeshore): Yep, thanks. We saw mixed results on the synthetic suite, TTFT still spiking at the 95th.
[00:34] Samir (SE): Right, and I think there's two things: first token latency looked better with streaming enabled but CPU jitter on app side added variability, and second the kernel variant we switched to (variant A) helps throughput but worse TTFT for short seq.
[01:05] Carlos: Can you remind me, TTFT numbers? I saw averages but want p95/p99.
[01:17] Samir: Sure, quick readout - avg token latency roughly 12ms, TTFT avg 180ms, p95 ~420ms, p99 ~820ms on our canary with 1x A100 equivalent. These are with sequence length capped at 1024 and batching at 8.
[01:42] Priya (SRE): Those p99s are the problem for the user journey where we need first response under 500.
[01:51] Jordan: Totally. Two knobs we proposed: try kernel variant B (different matmul kernel, traded throughput for TTFT) and enabling stream-priority which pushes early tokens out as soon as they decode. Also lower max seqlen on the critical route to 256.
[02:18] Maya: About streaming - last time when we turned on the stream option, we saw partial outputs earlier, but some clients had trouble re-assembling, flaky with our websocket proxy.
[02:33] Jordan: Understood - that's a client-side assembly issue. We can provide a small shim code snippet, and Redwood can run a hybrid mode where we produce smaller chunk sizes so proxies behave.
[02:50] Leah (CSM): I'll drop the shim in the drive link after call, so Priya's team can evaluate.
[03:00] Speaker 1: Also, quick question on quantization - were we still running int8-nq? The bench sheet shows q4 but notes mention int8 in some runs.
[03:14] Samir: There was a mix - earlier runs used q4_0, later we tried int8 to test memory pressure. int8 improved throughput but increased kernel overhead and slightly worsened TTFT because of extra dequant steps.
[03:33] Carlos: So perhaps stick with q4 for now? We care more about TTFT than max throughput.
[03:40] Samir: I'd agree, q4_0 plus kernel B seems like the sweet spot per our internal tests.
[03:48] Maya: How about sequence length distribution - our prod traffic is 80% sub-200 tokens but 20% are long sessions >2000.
[04:02] Jordan: Important callout - we can route by policy: keep the critical low-latency route on a pinned model config with seqlen cap 256 and streaming; route long sessions to a batched background pool (dedicated) where throughput matters. That will keep the user-facing TTFT tight.
[04:30] Priya: Routing is appealing but we need VPC and audit logs for those pinned pools. Are logs captured with private deployments?
[04:40] Jordan: Yes, for Dedicated and Private we enable audit logs and KMS integration. Note - internal doc sometimes spells KMS as K M S in transcripts, but we do support customer K M S and H S M flows.
[04:57] Maya: Ok. Practically, what's the switching cost for routing? Reconfig time?
[05:06] Samir: Can be immediate at config layer; for Dedicated you may need capacity prep (30-60 mins) but for hosted it's just policy change and the request router will start steering.
[05:20] Carlos: I want to understand the kernel choices more. What does kernel B change?
[05:26] Samir: Kernel B uses a tiled attention matmul optimized for small seq and low-latency -- it reduces first-token compute by avoiding some large fused ops. The trade is slightly lower sustained throughput for very long sequences. In some runs it cut TTFT p95 from ~420ms to ~260ms.
[05:46] Maya: That's promising. Did you test with our prompt templates? Some of ours have long instruction sections which inflate seqlen even for short replies.
[05:56] Samir: We ran a subset with your 'transactional-summary' prompt, which has a 300-token instruction plus 50 token user. When we trimmed instruction to 128 via lensing, TTFT improved a lot. Suggest prompt rewrite + model side seq cap for best results.
[06:20] Speaker 1: Lensing?
[06:23] Maya: sorry, redwood term - prompt lensing, basically compressing instructions or precomputing context in embeddings.
[06:30] Jordan: Also a reminder - prefix caching (K V cache) can help but only for repeated contexts. Our logs show limited repeated prefix patterns, so caching impact is modest but worth enabling where applicable.
[06:47] Leah: Quick pause - has anyone validated the client-side baseline? I.e., load balancer timeout, websocket proxy, and JVM GC causing spikes.
[06:58] Priya: We saw a GC at 10:08 yesterday that aligned with a p99 spike. We're fixing JVM tuning. Once fixed, sigma of latency improved.
[07:12] Samir: Good. For the bench we want a clean client baseline. Jordan, can you confirm the bench runner config?
[07:19] Jordan: Yeah - we'll run the 1k synthetic query run with the Lakeshore prompt set, 60% short, 40% long, capturing TTFT, p50/p95/p99, throughput, and token cost. We'll run three permutations: (1) q4 + kernel A + no streaming, (2) q4 + kernel B + streaming small-chunks, (3) int8 + kernel B + streaming.
[07:44] Maya: How long will that take?
[07:46] Jordan: Each run ~20 minutes but we can parallelize on two canaries, aiming to finish in one hour. We'll report back.
[07:55] Carlos: We also need a canary plan for production. Minimum rollback criteria?
[07:59] Samir: Canary targets: p95 TTFT < 300ms, error rate < 0.1%, and no customer-facing degradations for 30m. If fail, auto-fallback to previous model variant.
[08:14] Priya: Who triggers fallback? Is it automatic?
[08:19] Samir: We have automated SLO monitors that can trigger fallback; we can also require manual approval. We'll set it to manual for initial canary.
[08:27] Leah: I'll note that in the runbook.
[08:31] Speaker 1: Anything on pricing impact if we switch kernels and enable streaming?
[08:36] Jordan: Streaming slightly increases request counts but reduces perceived latency; cost delta minimal for short responses. Kernel B may lower throughput which could raise unit-cost for high-traffic long sessions, but routing mitigates that by sending long sessions elsewhere. We'll include cost delta in the bench spreadsheet.
[08:55] Maya: Ok good. A couple of fiddly things - we need RBAC scoped keys for the canary teams, and reviewer audit.
[09:04] Jordan: We can provision scoped API keys and set RBAC roles. For audit, we'll include the logs link.
[09:12] Carlos: Also legal will want SOC 2 status and retention policies. Do we have the security pack?
[09:17] Leah: Yes, I'll re-share the SOC2 + ISO pack and K M S docs.
[09:23] Maya: Back to tuning: I want to try lowering batch size to 4 on the low-latency pool in addition to kernel B. Any downside?
[09:32] Samir: Lower batch reduces batching latency but might underutilize GPU memory; kernel B is more efficient for small batch so it's fine. We'll measure token-cost per response.
[09:42] Jordan: OK action items are: run 3 bench permutations, enable streaming shim and share client snippet, provision scoped keys, and prepare canary runbook and roll-back criteria.
[10:00] Maya: When can we expect results?
[10:03] Jordan: We'll run them today and share spreadsheet by EOD Pacific.
[10:08] Carlos: Then next sync?
[10:10] Jordan: Next weekly check-in same time next Tuesday, unless we need an ad-hoc canary review.
[10:16] Priya: One more: are there any known issues with our on-prem firewall and streaming chunks?
[10:22] Samir: Sometimes enterprise firewalls reassemble chunks poorly; small increase in chunk timeout helps. We'll include network checklist.
[10:31] Speaker 1: Thanks all.
[10:33] Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up.
